title: Bitmask DP: State as a Subset
summary: DP where the state is an integer's bits representing a subset of a small universe — via Held-Karp TSP and worker-task assignment, the standard tool once n is small enough that 2^n is affordable.

slides.markdown:
Bitmask DP encodes "which elements have I used so far, out of a small universe" as a single integer, where bit `k` being set means element `k` is included. It's viable specifically because a small universe (roughly `n <= 20`) keeps `2^n` — the number of possible subsets — computationally affordable.

This unlocks DP over problems whose state genuinely is "a subset" — the traveling salesman problem, assigning workers to tasks, covering a small set with pieces — where no simpler 1D or 2D index captures what's needed. The signature tell that a problem wants this technique: a small `n` in the constraints (often explicitly `n <= 15` to `n <= 20`) paired with a question about orderings or assignments over the *entire* small set.

An integer `mask` represents a subset of `{0, 1, ..., n-1}`: bit `k` of `mask` is 1 exactly when element `k` is in the subset. `mask = 0` is the empty set; `mask = (1 << n) - 1` is the full set — all `n` elements included.

This works because a subset of a small, fixed universe has a natural one-to-one correspondence with a binary number: `n` yes/no decisions, one per bit. It's the same idea as `bitmask-subsets` in the bit-manipulation group, applied here specifically as a **DP state** rather than just an enumeration target — the difference this topic explores is what it means to cache an answer per subset and build up subset by subset.

slides.subTitle: (mask, current position)
slides.markdown:
For problems about visiting or assigning items one at a time, mask alone often isn't enough — you also need to know *where you currently are*, since the next step's cost usually depends on the current position, not just which elements have been used.

`dp[mask][last]` = the best (usually cheapest) way to have visited exactly the elements in `mask`, ending specifically at position `last`. This lets the recurrence ask "from here, which not-yet-used element should I go to next" and reuse the answer for any other path that happened to visit the same set of elements and land at the same final position — regardless of what order got there.

Adding one more element to a subset is a single bitwise OR: `new_mask = mask | (1 << k)` sets bit `k` without disturbing any other bit. Checking whether element `k` is already in the set is `mask & (1 << k)`.

<<< Image: a row of bits representing mask 01011 (5 bits, bits 0, 1, and 3 set); show it OR'd with a mask having only bit 2 set (00100), producing 01111, with each bit position labelled with its element number 4 down to 0 >>>

These two operations — check membership, add a member — are the entire mechanical vocabulary bitmask DP transitions use; there's no more exotic bit trick required beyond what `bit-idioms` already covers.

Every transition in bitmask DP moves from a mask to a **strictly larger** mask (setting one more bit, so `new_mask > mask` as an integer, since the added bit only increases the value). That means iterating `mask` from 0 up to `2^n - 1` in plain numeric order automatically guarantees every submask a given mask depends on has already been computed.

This is the bitmask-DP equivalent of "fill by increasing interval length" from interval DP — a different fill-order rule, but the same underlying requirement: **the loop order must match the recurrence's dependency direction.** No special sorting or separate submask enumeration is needed just to get the fill order right; the numeric order already does it, because adding a bit can never produce a smaller number.

`2^n` grows brutally fast: `2^20` is about a million, `2^30` is over a billion. Bitmask DP is only viable while `2^n` (times whatever per-mask work is needed) fits comfortably in your time and memory budget — practically, that ceiling sits around `n <= 20`, sometimes stretching to `n <= 25` with a very light per-mask cost.

Reaching for bitmask DP on a problem where `n` is in the hundreds or thousands is a category error — no amount of optimization saves an approach whose state space is fundamentally exponential in `n`. The check to make before committing: read the actual constraint on `n` in the problem statement. `n <= 20` is close to a direct hint to use this technique; `n <= 10^5` means something else entirely is expected, no matter how naturally the problem seems to describe subsets.

Assigning `n` workers to `n` tasks (minimizing total cost, one worker per task) uses a mask over **tasks already assigned**, processing workers one at a time in a fixed order: `dp[worker][mask]` = minimum cost to have assigned the first `worker` workers, using exactly the tasks in `mask`.

`dp[worker][mask] = min over each unassigned task t in mask of dp[worker-1][mask without t] + cost[worker][t]`. Because workers are processed in a fixed sequence (not chosen freely like TSP's next-city), this variant doesn't need a `last` position in its state — only the mask and which worker's turn it is. Recognizing which piece of state is genuinely needed (here: no `last`, because there's no notion of "current location") versus what TSP needed is exactly the kind of judgment interviewers are checking for.

| | Bitmask DP | Subset-enumeration backtracking |
|---|---|---|
| Revisits same subset via different orders | Caches and reuses | Recomputes every time |
| Complexity for TSP-style problems | O(n² * 2ⁿ) | O(n!) — much worse |
| When equivalent | If no state ever recurs across branches | Backtracking is then just as good, with less bookkeeping |

Both explore essentially the same space of subsets and orderings, but backtracking treats every path through that space as independent, while bitmask DP notices when two different paths arrive at the same `(mask, last)` and only pays for that state once. The gain — factorial down to exponential — is exactly the overlapping-subproblems payoff from the very first topic in this group, just with a subset as the state instead of an index.

Some bitmask DP transitions need to iterate all submasks of a given mask (subsets of an already-chosen subset), not just single-bit additions. The standard trick: starting from `sub = mask`, repeatedly set `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` until `sub` becomes 0 (processing 0 itself, then stopping) — this visits every submask of `mask` exactly once, in decreasing numeric order, in total time proportional to `3ⁿ` summed over all masks (a known, accepted bound for this pattern, not something to worry about improving further).

This shows up inside transitions like "try every way to split the current subset into a piece I handle now and a piece I defer" — a shape distinct from TSP's single-element extension, worth recognizing as a separate but related bitmask idiom.

slides.sectionTitle: Mask 0 needs its own base case
slides.markdown:
Mask `0` — nothing chosen yet — is a real state that needs an explicit, correct base value, not an assumption that it falls out of the general recurrence automatically. For TSP, `dp[mask][last]` needs a defined starting point like `dp[1][0] = 0` (only the start city visited, cost so far zero) rather than leaving `dp[0][...]` undefined and hoping the loop never touches it.

Forgetting this shows up as either an index error (reading an uninitialized `inf` and propagating it silently) or, worse, a `dp[0]` that defaults to `0` in every position when only one position (the actual start) should be reachable at the empty mask — an easy mistake in languages where arrays default-initialize to zero. Treat mask `0` (or whatever the true starting mask is for your problem) exactly as carefully as `dp[0]` or `dp[0][0]` gets treated in every earlier 1D and 2D DP topic in this group.
